title: "Where the leverage went: the graph engineer"
seoTitle: "The graph engineer: what graph engineering is, and where the leverage moved"
date: 2026-11-23
categories: ["ai"]
series: "Agent-native delivery"
unlisted: true
description: "A step should never grade its own work. Put the check in a different step."
cover: "/images/graph-engineer-cover.png"

We had a workflow that turned a design-system ticket into a merge request. It worked. Then I wanted the same thing for a second project, and I could not have it.

The agent inside the workflow was fine. The workflow itself was the problem. Every rule of the first project was built into its steps: which repository to touch, which branch to merge into, which checks to run, how to review. To use it anywhere else, we would have had to build it again.

That is when I saw where the leverage is now. The person who designs the workflow decides more about the result than the agent that runs inside it.

A workflow like this is a graph. Each step is a node. A node can be plain code, a call to a model, a tool, or a full coding agent. The arrows between the steps decide what happens next. Some arrows always go the same way. Some depend on a result.

## The graph we run

A ticket comes in. The intake step reads it and prepares the work. The plan step writes down what will change. The build step starts a coding agent in its own container, with the code cloned in. The agent works on a branch, pushes, and waits for the pipeline. The verdict step checks the pipeline result. The review step reads the changes. The last step opens a draft merge request. Then it comes to me.

Red goes back to the build, a limited number of times. From intake, a second edge marked needs info goes straight to the person without failing the run.</desc>

The first ticket through it cost less than a coffee. The pipeline went green after a few tries, and the agent fixed broken tests on its own along the way.

Then a second review, outside the platform, read the changes. The agent had also changed other buttons that nobody asked it to touch. The pipeline was green and the change was still wrong. That is why I care where the human sits in the graph.

## Shared steps, and one small workflow per project

The fix was not a bigger workflow. It was splitting it in two layers.

The first layer is the steps every project needs: intake, plan, build, pipeline verdict, review, finish. Each one is now a small workflow of its own, and every project uses the same ones.

The second layer is one short workflow per project. It does not do any work itself. It calls the shared steps in order and gives them the project's settings: which repository, which branch, which checks, and whether it may merge or only open a draft.

So a new project does not need a new graph. It needs a new set of settings.

We could have let each repository keep those settings in a file of its own. I said no. A repository should not be able to change the rules that decide what is done to it. The design system is allowed to merge into its development branch by itself. The platform repository only ever gets a draft that a person merges. That difference sits in one place, and I control it.

## Do not trust the agent's own report

The build agent waits for the pipeline and fixes what fails. Then it says the pipeline is green.

The verdict step does not take its word for it. It checks the pipeline again, with plain code and no model. The agent's report is a claim. The check is the answer.

We do the same for visual checks. We planted mistakes in a button: a wrong colour, a typo in the label, and the wrong height. The vision models caught the colour and the typo. They all missed the height. So sizes are measured by code, against the values in the design. The model can look. The measurement decides.

A step should never grade its own work. Put the check in a different step, one that cannot be talked into anything.

## The real question

For every step, ask one thing. Does the model decide here, or does the system decide for it?

Some work has a known shape. A design-system task is like that. The design gives the values, the spec says which files change, and the checks are always the same. We know every step and their order, so we draw all of it. The model only does the work inside each step.

Other work has no known shape. A bug report written in plain words can touch one file or many. It may need to be reproduced first. It may be in the front end or the back end. If we try to draw every case, we never finish. So the agent gets a goal, a working copy of the code, and a check that tells it when it is done. How it gets there is up to the agent.

The graph around that agent can still be big. Ours finds the right project, asks a person when it is unsure, picks up a merge request that already exists, reviews the plan, and loops until the acceptance criteria are met. All of that sits around the agent. The agent's own work stays open.

Where you know the shape of the work, draw it. Where you do not, give the model room.

## What the person drawing the graph owns

In the open case, the job comes down to this. The goal, and what the agent is allowed to see. The check that says it is done, strict enough that done and looking done are not the same thing. And the way out, for a run that cannot finish.

That is not much to draw. But it decides everything the agent is allowed to try, and better code inside a step cannot fix a bad boundary.

Writing code decides how one step behaves. Drawing the graph decides what the whole system may try, what counts as done, and what happens when it is not done. These used to be one job. They are two jobs now, and the second one is worth more.

## Where the money went

We ran the same ticket through the same planning step twice.

The first run was expensive. When I read it, most of the cost was waste. The whole conversation was sent again on every call. The planner loaded skills it did not need. It tried to download a ticket it already had, without the access to do it.

The model was not bad at planning. The graph gave it too much and let it try too much.

So we set rules around the step. The ticket is already in the prompt, so do not fetch it. Explore a little, then write. Load only the skills the task needs. We also moved to a cheaper model.

The second run cost a small fraction of the first and found the same fix in the same files. I cannot say how much came from the rules and how much from the model. We changed both at once.

## What crosses from one step to the next

At first we passed everything between steps: the full build output, the full review output. The last step broke. One large value had wiped out the others next to it.

Now only short facts cross between steps: the result, the merge request, the review decision. Everything else stays where it was made, and the next step reads it from there if it needs it.

My rule: if I cannot say why a piece of data goes from one step to the next, it does not go.

## Arrows that need care

**The retry.** When the pipeline fails, the build gets another try, but only a few. Without a limit, a flaky test and a stubborn model can keep going while everything looks fine from outside. A retry with a limit is engineering. A retry without one is a bill.

**The exit.** We had a loop that would not stop. The work finished, then the build started again and marked the ticket as failed. The work was done and the label said failed. A loop needs a clear exit, and each round has to start clean.

**The escape.** Before any code is written, a ticket can stop with "needs info": no project fits, or the problem is not in this code. It goes to a person without failing. If failing is the only way out, the model learns to pretend it finished.

## The human is a step too

I am a step in this graph, and the slowest one. I get a draft merge request, a pipeline result and a review. I decide to merge or not. At night, that can take hours.

The design-system flow has taken components from ticket to accepted with nobody involved. It still stops for me in two places: when a visual change needs a new reference image, and when code goes into the main branch. Those are not missing features. Those are the decisions I keep.

The platform's own review is not enough either. On one merge request it gave a top grade, and a second review found real problems it had missed. The extra buttons from the first ticket passed every step of the platform. A review outside it caught them.

So the checks in front of me must be real, and so must the claims about them. A fix once looked good after a few test runs. That is not proof. Proof is the logs, before and after, on enough runs.

## Where it goes wrong

The mistake is drawing too much, too specifically.

Our first design-system workflow was right for the design system and useless anywhere else, because one project's rules were built into its shape. Every arrow you draw is a decision you make for the model, on every input, forever. Draw too many and you have written the program you wanted the agent to write, in a worse language.

A simple test. Can you write the steps down in order before you see the ticket? If yes, draw them. If you keep writing "it depends", stop drawing and give the agent room.

## Still reading the diff

The agent wrote the code. The graph decided what it was allowed to touch.

I still read the diff.
